title: Charles Otto is remembered, Arthur Ellis is missed and septic clogs the Senate, in political notes
summary: Lawmakers make some noise about a quiet former colleague, Del. Charles Otto, Sen. Arthur Ellis makes his congressional campaign kickoff, and a bill on septic systems that was clogging Senate progress gets flushed back to committee.
content:
by William J. Ford, Maryland Matters March 24, 2026

by William J. Ford, Maryland Matters March 24, 2026

The late Del. Charles Otto (R-Lower Shore) didn’t speak much in his 14 years in the legislature. But his colleagues spoke plenty on his behalf Monday.

The House voted 137-1 Monday to create the Charles J. Otto Agricultural Education Promise Act, which establishes the Maryland Fair and Agricultural Education Promise Fund. It would allocate $200,000 annually for two groups: $100,000 to the Maryland Agricultural Education Foundation Inc. “to promote and enhance statewide agricultural education”; and another $100,000 for the Maryland FFA Association “for agricultural education and career development.”

But not before a dozen lawmakers, from both sides of the aisle, spent 15 minutes on one of the busiest days of the legislative session remembering Otto, who died suddenly in October and was known for his knowledge of agricultural issues and advocacy for the Eastern Shore.

“Passage of this bill represents a bipartisan, team effort,” said Del. April Miller (R-Frederick), the lead sponsor of House Bill 972. “With our vote today, we are able to memorialize one of our own. A man that did have a smile a mile wide, was always quick with a joke, a kind word and was a tireless advocate for agriculture and the Eastern Shore.”

Miller said the bill was led by students at Middletown High School to support agricultural education.

Then the recollections began.

House Minority Leader Jason Buckel (R-Allegany) called Otto a “decent, kind and talented man.” Del. Diana Fennell (D-Prince George’s) said she and Otto had dinner every Tuesday for 11 years, talking about farming.

“This is so, so beautiful to be done in recognition of my good friend, Del. Otto,” Fennell said.

Del. Deni Taveras (D-Prince George’s) said she and Otto were good friends, even though they constantly disagreed on politics.

“We have very opposing points of view, but we would sit every night and we would have dinner together for years since I came here,” Taveras said. “We would fight. We would kiss and make up. And we would fight, and we would kiss and make up. At the end of the day, it just came we had more in common than we had [differences].”

Not all the memories were heartfelt. The comments began with Del. Tom Hutchinson (R-Middle Shore), who said he was supplying the entire Eastern Shore delegation with Otto’s “favorite floor snack, beef jerky. Or as he would refer to it as, ‘horse ass.’”

The bill now heads to the Senate, which does not have its own version of the bill. If approved, the act would go into effect June 1.

When the Senate was plowing through bills Monday night, in attempt to beat the crossover deadline for legislation, Sen. Arthur Ellis (D-Charles) was almost an hour away in Indian Head, attending a twice-postponed kickoff for his bid for Congress.

He wasn’t the only senator absent Monday night: Sens. Joanne C. Benson (D-Prince George’s), Mary Dulany-James (D-Harford) and Bryan Simonaire (R-Anne Arundel) were also not present. But Ellis — who staged a one-man protest earlier in the session by refusing to register his presence in the chamber for floor sessions — was the only one whose campaign put out notice that he would be attending a political event.

Ellis said the event, officially kicking off his campaign to enter the crowded race to replace retiring Rep. Steny Hoyer (D-5th), had already been rescheduled twice, including a day when a snowstorm hit the state last month.

“Every now and again you have to make sacrifices for the jobs you have coming on,” Ellis said in a brief phone interview more than two hours before the Senate convened at 7:14 p.m. Monday. “I did a lot of sacrifice in the military, a disabled veteran. Service of country. I’m still making sacrifices.”

Ellis’ kickoff formally makes him one of about two dozen Democrats seeking to replace Hoyer, who decided not to seek reelection after serving on Capitol Hill for more than 40 years. Hoyer has endorsed Del. Adrian Boafo (D-Prince George’s) at a joint campaign appearance March 2.

But that endorsement has done little to dissuade the crowded field of congressional wannabes. In addition to Ellis and Boafo, other high-profile Democrats seeking the seat include Del. Nicole Williams (D-Prince George’s), Charles County Board of Commissioners President Reuben Collins II, Prince George’s County Councilmember Wala Blegay, former U.S. Capitol Police Officer Harry Dunn — who finished second in a 22-candidate Democratic primary field in 2024 for the 3rd District seat now held by Rep. Sarah Elfreth — and former Prince George’s County Executive Rushern L. Baker III.

In his absence, the Senate gave final approval to about two dozen bills during the second session Monday night on crossover day, the theoretical last day for a bill to cross over to the other chamber and be guaranteed a hearing before the end of the session in three weeks.

One of the bills that Ellis might be thankful he missed was a second day of debate on Senate Bill 165, Sen. Benjamin Brooks’ (D-Baltimore County) bill that would impose new requirements on landlords to pump out and inspect septic systems before new tenants move in, and in accordance with this state environmental code.

Brooks said the bill is intended to protect the state’s waterways. But critics questioned whether septic systems really posed that much of a threat to the state’s waters, and they asked what the bill would do that current regulations don’t do.

To Sen. Jack Bailey (R-Calvert and St. Mary’s), understanding the difference between a working and a failing septic system is not that complicated.

“We all had a future before we came here and I actually was a sewage disposal contractor,” Bailey said of his pre-legislative life, “And I’d say that it was pretty easy, you know, you had to go take a test and … you pretty much realized that it went downhill.”

You knew the system was not working when the waste came up, instead of going down, he said.

His comments were part of a nearly half-hour debate on the bill, on one of the busiest days on the legislative calendar. That was in addition to debate Friday on the bill, when senators rejected an amendment from Senate Minority Whip Justin Ready (R-Frederick) and were debating another amendment by Senate Minority Leader Stephen Hershey (R-Upper Shore) when Sen. Brian Feldman (D-Montgomery) asked that debate on the bill be paused until Monday.

Senators Monday night had just defeated another amendment from Ready and were debating a Hershey amendment when Feldman, chair of the Education, Energy and the Environment Committee that handled the bill, called a retreat after 26 minutes of discussion on the bill Monday.

“Mr. President, we have in our possession in the committee, the cross-file [companion House bill] and I think that some of these issues we can engage in dialogue on the cross-file, so I’d move to recommit this back to the committee at this point and then we’ll work off the cross-file and maybe work through some of these issues,” Feldman said.

“Given the timing, I think that probably makes more sense,” said Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore City).
